svg.aria-label: Diagram: Amazon EBS snapshot lock blocks deletion and nothing else. AWS states that while a snapshot is locked it cannot be deleted by any user regardless of their IAM permissions, and in the next sentence that you can continue to use a locked snapshot in the same way that you would use any other snapshot. What the lock stops is deletion. What it leaves alone is everything that makes the snapshot useful: creating volumes from it, copying it, sharing it, archiving it, deregistering an associated AMI, and deleting the KMS key used to encrypt it. Read together, three considerations describe a reachable state in which a snapshot cannot be deleted by anyone for up to a hundred years and cannot be read either, because its key is gone. The four lock states are governance and compliance-cooloff, which block deletion but can be unlocked by users with permissions, compliance, which can neither be unlocked nor deleted and whose duration can only be increased, and expired, in which the snapshot is no longer locked and can be deleted. Compared with AWS Backup Vault Lock, the snapshot lock's cooling-off period of 1 to 72 hours is optional and can be omitted for immediate irreversibility, while the vault lock's grace time must be at least 3 days or 72 hours, so the vault lock's shortest grace period is the snapshot lock's longest. Both share the same escape hatch: closing the account suspends it for 90 days, after which AWS deletes the data even if it is locked.
svg.title: The lock defends the object's existence, and only that
svg.text: Read the sentence after the one everybody quotes.
EBS snapshot lock — a narrow guarantee, stated narrowly.
WHAT IT STOPS
“it can’t be deleted by any user, regardless of
their IAM permissions”
One operation. That is the whole guarantee, and it
holds against the account root.
WHAT IT LEAVES ALONE
“You can continue to use a locked snapshot in the
same way that you would use any other snapshot”
create volumes · copy · share · archive
deregister the AMI · delete the KMS key
Three considerations that are unremarkable alone
“You can delete the KMS key used to encrypt a locked snapshot.” • “You can deregister an AMI that has
associated snapshots that are locked.” • “The only way to delete a snapshot that is locked in compliance
mode before its lock expires is to close the associated AWS account.”
Together: undeletable for up to a century, and unreadable, because the key is gone.
Four states, one of them a one-way door
governance unlock: yes
compliance-cooloff unlock: yes
compliance unlock: NO
expired deletable again
In compliance, the duration can only be increased.
The reversible window, against the vault lock
Snapshot lock: “1 to 72 hours”, and optional — omit it
and the lock is irreversible from the first second.
Vault lock: “at least 3 days (72 hours)”, required.
The vault lock’s shortest grace period is the snapshot
lock’s longest.
AWS names the case it does not want you to use this for
“We recommend that you do not lock snapshots created by AWS Backup … we recommend that you use AWS Backup
Vault Lock.” Two retention systems on one object is two sources of truth, not twice the protection.
The audit: for every locked snapshot, find who can delete its KMS key.
That set of principals is the real blast radius of the retention control, and it is usually wider than the set
who could have deleted the snapshot before you locked it.
Same escape hatch as a locked vault: close the account, and after 90 days AWS deletes the data regardless.
